title: How Polar Bears Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore polar bears: their evolution from brown bears, physical adaptations (translucent hollow fur, blubber, webbed front paws, paw pads), size and lifespan, swimming, diet centered on ringed seals and breathing-hole hunting, induced ovulation and delayed implantation, mating and cub rearing, dwindling sea ice and population threats, human encounters and attacks (Churchill, Manitoba), managed hunting by Inuit and trophy hunters, the death of zoo bear Newt from autoimmune encephalitis, Inuit polar bear legends, and a listener mail about squatters' rights.

segments.title: Introduction to polar bears
segments.summary: Hosts banter about the intro and introduce polar bears as understudied, dangerous, huggable animals, and discuss their evolution from brown bears and interbreeding.

segments.title: Population, range and size
segments.summary: Discussion of the roughly 25,000 polar bears in nineteen populations across five countries, Arctic sea ice loss, and size and lifespan stats (males up to about 1,300 pounds, lifespan about 20 years).

segments.title: Physical adaptations
segments.summary: Hosts describe the polar bear's large paws that act as snowshoes, webbed front paws, paw pads, swimming ability, and endurance walking and swimming long distances.

segments.title: Fur, blubber and temperature tolerance
segments.summary: Explanation that the polar bear's fur is translucent and hollow, trapping air to insulate, so the bear looks white; blubber layer; small exposed extremities; tolerance of extreme cold.

segments.title: Mating, induced ovulation and gestation
segments.summary: Scientists are unsure how females signal readiness; females have induced ovulation and delayed implantation with an eight-month gestation. Females are first bred around six to eight years old and have about five litters in a lifetime.

segments.title: Cubs, denning and male behavior
segments.summary: Females dig snow dens to give birth and nurse cubs for at least about twenty months; cubs are born blind and toothless. Males do not kill each other over females, and males sometimes share meals; mother bears defend cubs fiercely.

segments.title: Ringed seal hunting at breathing holes
segments.summary: Ringed seals carve breathing holes in sea ice, and polar bears wait patiently by these holes to ambush them. Bears eat blubber, which provides omega-3 fats, then clean off blood and bathe in sea water or snow.

segments.title: Human encounters, attacks and hunting
segments.summary: Polar bears are apex predators that may wander into towns like Churchill, Manitoba, which has had two fatal attacks in about 300 years. US and Canada recorded eight fatal attacks since 1972 (per the hosts), half at zoos. Discussion of regulated hunting by Inuit and paid trophy hunters, and survival tips such as making yourself look big.

segments.title: Newt the polar bear and Inuit legends
segments.summary: Newt, a German zoo polar bear, died after a seizure; researchers diagnosed anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, an autoimmune disease, the first such diagnosis in an animal. Hosts also cover Inuit legends about polar bears as shape-shifters and the offering of tools after a kill, and the name Nanook.

segments.title: Listener mail: squatters' rights
segments.summary: Listener Elias asks whether squatters' rights could be claimed by renting and refusing to leave; hosts say it would take many years and the landlord would likely have them removed.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to social media, email, and the website for contacting the show.
